package_info.why_malicious: The package includes a compiled Python module (*.pyc) containing malicious code, distributed without the corresponding source file, and ensures its execution by importing it from the core module. This obfuscates the payload and bypasses standard static analysis, making the package intentionally deceptive and potentially harmful.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code imports the sneaky module, causing any code in sneaky.pyc to execute immediately upon package import.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Importing a module that only exists in compiled form is highly unusual and can be used to hide malicious payloads from static analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, all imported modules should have corresponding source files for transparency and review. Here, only the compiled version is present.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some proprietary packages may distribute only .pyc files to protect intellectual property, but this is rare in open-source ecosystems.
key_indicators: Import statement for a module with no source file
Triggering execution of obfuscated code at import-time

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: print("[!] Malware could have run here")
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the compiled code executes its payload, which could be any arbitrary Python code (demonstrated here as a print statement, but could be malicious actions in real attacks).

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The .pyc file is distributed without its source, making it difficult to audit. The code is executed automatically when the package is imported.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not execute hidden, unauditable code on import.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, .pyc-only modules are used for code obfuscation in commercial/proprietary software.
key_indicators: Presence of .pyc file without matching .py source
Automatic execution of code from compiled module

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At build/distribution-time, the setup script is configured to include all .pyc files in the distributed package, ensuring the compiled malicious module is shipped to users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Explicitly including .pyc files in package_data is uncommon and can be used to distribute obfuscated or malicious code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard practice is to distribute source files, not just compiled bytecode.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some proprietary vendors may distribute .pyc files for obfuscation, but this is not standard for open-source packages.
key_indicators: Explicit inclusion of .pyc files in package_data

attack_chain.action: Malicious Python code is written in a source file (sneaky.py) and compiled to .pyc.
attack_chain.leads_to: Obfuscated payload is ready for distribution.

attack_chain.action: The source file (sneaky.py) is deleted, leaving only the compiled .pyc file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Only obfuscated code remains in the package.

attack_chain.action: setup.py is configured to include .pyc files in the package distribution.
core.py imports the sneaky module, triggering execution of the .pyc payload at import-time.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code executes automatically when the package is imported.

behavioral_signatures: Import-time execution of code from .pyc-only modules
Presence of import statements for modules lacking .py source files
Distribution of packages with .pyc files but missing corresponding .py files
file_indicators: Absence of matching .py source for included .pyc files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan package distributions for .pyc files that do not have corresponding .py source files. Flag packages where setup.py or MANIFEST includes '*.pyc' in package_data. Monitor for import statements in code that reference modules only present as .pyc files. Alert on packages that execute code from .pyc-only modules at import-time, as this is a strong indicator of obfuscated or malicious behavior.
